entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: By the end of this module you can
entries.text:
Tell strong multi-factor authentication (MFA) from weak,
 and move off SMS to an authenticator app (TOTP) or a
 hardware key. Harden your home network: the router admin login, WPA3
 encryption, and an isolated guest network. Verify out of band before acting on anything about
 money, passwords or access. Keep up the daily habits - BYOD patching, password
 management, and reporting an incident fast.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: There is no perimeter now
entries.text:
An office has a wall around it: corporate firewalls,
 intrusion detection, locked doors. Remote work removes it. Work travels over home Wi-Fi, personal routers and
 commercial mobile networks. So every device is its own perimeter, which takes technical
 hardening and steady personal habits.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: MFA, weakest to strongest
entries.text:
MFA helps beyond a password, but the methods are not equal. SMS codes - vulnerable. A texted
 code can be intercepted by SIM-swapping, mobile malware,
 or a smishing lure. Authenticator apps (TOTP) -
 recommended. Time-based One-Time Password apps
 - Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator,
 1Password - generate the code on your device, with
 no cellular SMS involved. FIDO2 hardware keys - the gold
 standard. A physical USB or NFC key such as a
 YubiKey is phishing-resistant: it binds the login
 cryptographically to the verified site domain.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: Home network and your own devices (BYOD)
entries.text:
Wi-Fi is an easy side door into work systems. Change the router’s default
 login. Factory passwords like
 admin/admin are public knowledge, and
 botnets scan for them constantly. Use WPA3, or WPA2 Enterprise. Strong
 encryption only - turn off outdated WEP and plain
 WPA. Put IoT devices on the guest network. Smart TVs, appliances and cameras often go unpatched. Keep the work laptop on an isolated guest network so a
 compromised gadget cannot intercept work traffic. Let updates install themselves. Operating system, browser, security software. Unpatched
 software is how a drive-by download reaches you from a
 page you only visited.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: Verify out of band
entries.text:
Make it a personal rule: anything unexpected about money, a
 password reset, an access grant, or a transfer of sensitive
 data gets confirmed on a second channel. Example: a client emails new bank details
 for your invoices. Call them - on the number from the
 earlier paper contract, never the one on the new invoice.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: If it already happened, speed wins
entries.text:
Clicked a suspicious link, typed credentials into a
 questionable site, downloaded an untrusted file? Time is
 critical. Disconnect the device from Wi-Fi or Ethernet at once, to
 stop malware moving sideways or commands running
 remotely. Report it to your IT security team or client contact. Early reporting lets them revoke compromised tokens
 before the attacker pivots deeper in.

entries.title: Safe Practices for Remote Work: Red flags
entries.text:
SMS-only MFA. Text passcodes instead of an
 authenticator app or a hardware key. A default router password. Home Wi-Fi still
 on the factory admin login. One network for work and the smart home. The work laptop on the same Wi-Fi subnet as unpatched IoT
 devices. Updates put off for weeks. Pending
 operating system and browser security patches.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona
entries.text:
Who this is for: remote workers handling
 administrative data, HR workflows, customer records, vendor
 management, or client onboarding.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: By the end of this module you can
entries.text:
Explain the slow-burn structure of pretexting, where
 phishing goes straight for panic. Recognise the usual personas: a fake external auditor, a
 new vendor, an HR representative, a distressed
 contractor. Notice the quiet moves that steer you around identity
 checks and the ticketing system. Hold a verification step for any unannounced request for
 administrative or directory data.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: What pretexting is
entries.text:
Pretexting is social engineering with a script. The attacker
 invents a situation - the pretext - and a person
 to go with it, then uses that character to talk you out of
 confidential information or unauthorised access. A phishing email wants instant panic. Pretexting is
 patient - a slow-burn approach:
 casual exchanges first, over days or weeks, rapport and
 credibility built, the request last.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: The personas
entries.text:
Attackers research real roles so the character fits. The external auditor or compliance
 officer. An urgent “data privacy
 audit” or “software licensing check”
 that needs your directory charts, system architecture
 documents, or employee listings. The new vendor or subcontractor. A
 newly hired third-party provider who needs
 “sample data files” or access to your
 internal staging servers before an upcoming project. The distressed remote colleague. A
 fellow remote employee locked out while travelling,
 appealing to your sympathy so you share internal files
 or forward login details.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: Getting around the process
entries.text:
Pretexters lean on ordinary decency - politeness,
 wanting to help, deference to authority - to talk you
 past your procedures. Away from the ticket. They discourage a
 formal IT ticket or an administrative review:
 “Opening a ticket takes 3 days, and the VP needs
 this file in 10 minutes.”
 Flattery and sympathy. You are made to
 feel like the one helpful person who can rescue this.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: Scenario: the fake HR benefits survey
entries.text:
David, a remote administrative assistant, gets a LinkedIn
 connection request and message from “Elena, Senior HR
 Director at Global HR Solutions”: “Hi
 David, your company has contracted us to review remote
 employee benefit satisfaction. We are conducting brief
 5-minute interviews.” 
 Over three days of polite messaging, Elena builds rapport. On day four she sends an “Employee Verification
 Portal” link and asks David to confirm his corporate
 ID, home address, and his manager’s email. It felt
 natural, so he submits the data without checking with his
 own HR department.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: What to do instead
entries.text:
Keep it in the ticket system. Administrative, data and access requests go through the
 official, authenticated queue - no exceptions for
 urgency. Check third parties yourself. If an
 external auditor or vendor contacts you, confirm their
 contract status with your manager or procurement lead
 before sharing files. Distrust the elaborate story. Real
 company business rarely needs a complicated explanation
 for skipping a standard security check.

entries.title: Pretexting: the Fake Persona: Red flags
entries.text:
Unsolicited contact over several days. Casual rapport first, a request for data or files later. Pressure to avoid official channels. No
 ticket, no official distribution list, no manager involved. Questions about how you work. Casual
 interest in your organisational hierarchy, software
 versions, or internal tools. Appeals to empathy or authority. Extreme
 distress, impending disciplinary action, or an executive
 deadline, used to force compliance.

entries.title: Phishing and QR Code Scams: By the end of this module you can
entries.text:
Spot the giveaways in a phishing email: a lookalike domain,
 a faked sender, a deadline. Explain how a link hidden in a QR code - quishing
 - slips past a Security Email Gateway (SEG). Run the same three checks before clicking a link, scanning
 a QR code, or typing a password into a portal.

entries.title: Phishing and QR Code Scams: Phishing when the office is in the cloud
entries.text:
In an office your computer sits behind a company firewall, an
 intrusion prevention system (IPS), and a monitored Security
 Email Gateway (SEG). Working remotely, you connect straight to
 Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or Slack over home Wi-Fi, often
 on your own device (BYOD). None of that is in the way, so
 attacks arrive dressed as the tools you open daily. The fake sites lean on domain tricks. Typosquatting swaps one
 character: micros0ft-verify.com for
 microsoft.com . Combosquatting adds
 trusted-sounding words, as in
 slack-login-security.net .

entries.title: Phishing and QR Code Scams: Phishing when the office is in the cloud
entries.text:
And because an SSL/TLS
 certificate is free, the counterfeit server shows the same
 HTTPS padlock as the real one - which is what convinces
 people the login page is safe. Traditional phishing sends a clickable link the gateway can scan. Quishing hides it in a QR code image the gateway cannot read, opened on an unmonitored personal phone.

entries.title: Phishing and QR Code Scams: Quishing: the link inside a QR code
entries.text:
Email filters read text - the written HTML and any
 plain-text URL. They rarely run OCR (optical character
 recognition) on an image, or decode a picture inside a PDF
 attachment. A Quick Response (QR) code is an image, so the link
 inside it is invisible to them. That is why quishing keeps
 growing against distributed staff. The email claims to be an “MFA Security Update” or
 an “HR Employee Handbook Review,” so the gateway
 lets it through. You scan it with your phone camera.

entries.title: Phishing and QR Code Scams: Quishing: the link inside a QR code
entries.text:
The
 session moves off your monitored work computer onto an
 unmonitored personal device, landing on a credential-harvesting
 web form, or an OAuth page asking you to grant consent.

entries.title: Phishing and QR Code Scams: Red flags
entries.text:
A display name reading “IT Helpdesk” over a
 header address of
 support@mail-system-update24.net . Subject lines built on fear: “Urgent: Account
 Suspension in 2 Hours.” “Unusual Login Detected
 - Verify Immediately.”
 An unsolicited QR code, to be scanned on your phone to
 reach a desktop web service. A greeting of “Dear Customer,” or link text
 reading portal.company.com that points at an
 unrelated IP address.

entries.title: Phishing and QR Code Scams: The three checks
entries.text:
Read the real address. Hover over the
 sender’s name for the full address, and match the
 domain to official company records. Never scan a code you were sent. To log in
 or reset a password, type the official portal address into
 a browser yourself. Report, then contain. Hit “Report
 Phishing” in your mail client. If you entered your
 details, tell your security team and change that password
 across connected systems.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages
entries.text:
Who this is for: remote employees and freelancers
 using a personal phone (BYOD) for multi-factor authentication
 (MFA), client messaging, and team communication.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: By the end of this module you can
entries.text:
Explain why a text feels more trustworthy than an email,
 and why that is a problem. Recognise the technical tricks: shortened URLs, a spoofed
 sender ID, a fake portal. Tell a real bank or courier alert apart from a smishing
 lure. Harden your phone, protect your OTP and MFA codes, and
 report what arrives.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: Why the phone is the soft spot
entries.text:
Smishing is phishing by text - a malicious link or a
 prompt to call, sent over Short Message Service (SMS) or an app
 like WhatsApp, Signal or Telegram. As Multi-Factor
 Authentication (MFA) and team collaboration move onto phones,
 so do the attackers. A phone has three specific weaknesses:
 You trust it more. Text feels personal, so
 texts get opened and tapped far more than email. You cannot see the link. A mobile browser
 has no room for the full URL, hiding the real destination
 domain. Nothing is watching. A personal phone
 usually lacks the company’s endpoint detection and
 response (EDR) agent or web filtering.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: The lures that work
entries.text:
Each lure is built on an ordinary, everyday event:
 The parcel. A FedEx, DHL or postal
 delivery stuck until you confirm an address or pay a small
 fee. The link harvests your card or password. The bank alert. An urgent security hold or
 unauthorised transaction on your account, and a link to
 “click here immediately to verify identity”. The OTP grab. The attacker logs into your
 corporate account, which sends a real One-Time Password
 (OTP) to your phone. Then a text arrives: “IT Desk:
 We detected suspicious activity. Reply with the 6-digit
 code sent to your device to secure your account.”
 The code is real; the sender is not.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: Hidden links, faked senders
entries.text:
The true destination hides behind a URL shortener -
 bit.ly , tinyurl.com ,
 t.co - or a lookalike domain like
 bank-secure-login.site . Sender ID spoofing goes
 further: an SMS gateway tool sets the alpha-numeric sender name
 to your bank’s, so the fake text drops into the exact
 same conversation thread as the real ones.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: Scenario: the IT unlocking text
entries.text:
Sarah is a remote customer support agent. At 8:00 AM a text
 arrives: “OKTA ALERT: Your remote access account has
 been flagged for compliance review. Resolve within 30 minutes
 to maintain shift access:
 https://okta-sso-verify.link/login ” 
 Afraid of missing her shift and being disciplined, she taps the
 link. The page is an exact copy of her company’s SSO
 login portal. She enters her username, password and push MFA
 token, handing her enterprise credentials to an attacker.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: What to do
entries.text:
Do not tap links in unsolicited texts. Treat every clickable link as untrusted. If the alert
 claims to be your bank or employer, open their official app
 or site yourself. Guard your OTPs and MFA codes. Never share
 a One-Time Password or MFA token with anyone, by text or by
 phone. Real IT never asks for one back. Expand short links first. Use a URL
 expansion tool, or your phone’s link preview, before
 tapping a shortened link. Report it. Forward scam texts to SPAM
 ( 7726 ) on networks that support it, or tell
 your security team.

entries.title: Smishing: Scam Texts and Messages: Red flags
entries.text:
A text threatening account suspension, a missed delivery or
 legal action unless you tap now. A shortened or obscured link - bit.ly ,
 tiny.cc - or an unusual top-level domain
 like .xyz , .site ,
 .info . Anyone asking you to text back or read aloud a multi-factor
 authentication code. A bank or corporate alert from a standard 10-digit mobile
 number instead of a registered shortcode.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research
entries.text:
Who this is for: remote staff with system access,
 administrative privileges, financial responsibilities, or a public
 social media profile.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: By the end of this module you can
entries.text:
Tell broad mass phishing apart from a message written for
 you alone. Recognise how Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) from
 LinkedIn, GitHub and X becomes a personal lure. Spot the risk in a macro-enabled attachment, a double file
 extension, and a move to an out-of-band messaging channel.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: How it differs from mass phishing
entries.text:
Mass phishing sends thousands of identical, generic messages
 broadly, hoping a small percentage click. Spear phishing is the
 opposite: one message, aimed at one person, team or
 organisation. It names real people, your current client engagement, the
 internal platforms you use, a recent company event. That
 familiarity drops your guard. Details from LinkedIn, GitHub and social media/X combine into one message aimed at a single target.

entries.title: Spear Phishing and Target Research: The attachment
entries.text:
The payload arrives as a file, weaponised in one of three ways:
 Macro-enabled Office documents 
 ( .docm , .xlsm ). Enable macros and
 an embedded Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) script
 downloads secondary malware - a trojan or
 infostealer. Double extensions ( .pdf.exe ,
 .docx.iso ). Operating systems hide known
 extensions by default, so
 Quarterly_Report.pdf.exe shows on screen as
 Quarterly_Report.pdf . Encrypted archives ( .zip ,
 .rar , .7z ). The archive is
 locked, the password is in the email body, and the gateway
 cannot look inside - so the attachment walks past the
 automated perimeter scanners.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone
entries.text:
Who this is for: remote workers in client
 support, phone-based operations, sales, executive support, or
 administrative roles.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: By the end of this module you can
entries.text:
Explain how caller ID spoofing and VoIP let a stranger
 look internal. Describe how a live call overloads you into complying. Recognise the usual stories: a fake IT helpdesk, an
 emergency hold on your money, an urgent
 remote-management install. Call back on a number you looked up yourself, before
 sharing credentials or approving access.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: What vishing is
entries.text:
Vishing is phishing over a phone call or a Voice over IP
 (VoIP) line. The caller wants sensitive data, financial
 details, or access to a system. An email you can reread; a
 live call you answer in real time. That pressure is the
 point.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: Faking the number
entries.text:
Phone protocols let a caller choose what your screen shows. Caller ID spoofing. Web-based VoIP
 services let an attacker set the outbound caller ID to
 anything: an internal extension like “Corporate IT
 Helpdesk” or “HQ Executive Office”, or
 your bank’s customer service line. Interactive Voice Response (IVR)
 robocalls. An automated menu (“Press 1 to
 speak to our fraud department”) imitates a real
 bank call centre, then routes you to a live scammer.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: Why a live call works
entries.text:
The caller hears your tone and your hesitation, and adapts. Manufactured urgency. A cyberattack or
 a fraudulent transaction is happening right now, so you
 must act now. Borrowed authority. The caller plays a
 senior systems administrator, a financial auditor, an
 executive assistant - someone you do not argue
 with. No thinking room. A fast pace stops you
 stepping back to judge whether any of this is true.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: The calls remote workers actually get
entries.text:
The password reset. Your remote access
 account has suspicious logins, says the caller. Read out
 the code in your SMS, or approve the push notification. The urgent patch. Your laptop needs a
 fix now: download and run remote administration software
 - AnyDesk, TeamViewer, Quick Assist. Once
 installed, the caller controls your workstation.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: Scenario: the fake IT helpdesk
entries.text:
Push bombing a tired engineer. Mark, a remote systems engineer, gets 15 MFA push
 notifications at 10 PM. His phone rings. The caller ID says
 “Internal IT Operations.”
 “Hi Mark, Dave from IT SecOps. Those push alerts
 are a gateway glitch. I am pushing one final prompt -
 tap Approve to clear the queue so your account isn’t
 locked overnight.” 
 Tired, Mark taps Approve. Dave was an attacker who already
 had his password; the call plus push fatigue got him past
 MFA.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: What to do instead
entries.text:
Never read out a credential or a code. Real IT will not ring and ask for your password, PIN, or
 MFA code. Hang up and call back. If the caller
 claims to be an internal department or your bank, end
 the call. Look up the official number in the company
 directory or on the back of your card, and dial it
 yourself. Refuse remote-access installs. Never
 install AnyDesk or TeamViewer because an inbound call
 told you to.

entries.title: Vishing: Phishing by Phone: Red flags
entries.text:
An unsolicited technical support call. Someone claiming to be internal IT, wanting system access or
 your password. A push to install remote access tools. AnyDesk, TeamViewer or LogMeIn, during an unexpected call. A request to confirm MFA. Approve this push
 notification, or read me your one-time password. Pressure and intimidation. Aggressive
 language, or threats of dismissal or legal action if you
 refuse.
